session_meta.research_objective:
Focus group guide exploring how men in the UK make everyday food
choices, how social context, work, hobbies, health, taste and other
people shape what they eat, how gender and masculinity may influence
food choices, and what would need to change for plant-based foods to
become more acceptable or appealing.
session_meta.topic_domain: Masculinity, food choice, animal product consumption, and plant-based eating
session_meta.participant_collective_identity: Men in the UK reflecting on food choices, male friendship, gender norms, and plant-based eating
session_meta.moderator_knowledge_brief:
Explore (1) everyday food decision-making, (2) the social contexts in
which men spend time with male friends, (3) the influence of other
people, work, hobbies, health, nutrition and taste on food choices,
(4) whether participants perceive gender as shaping what they eat,
(5) social acceptability and gendered meanings attached to vegetarian,
vegan, plant-based, feminine or masculine foods, and (6) what personal,
social and practical changes would make plant-based eating more viable
or appealing. The discussion should remain exploratory, non-judgmental,
and non-leading.

initial_session_plan.thematisation_approach: These participants are men in their twenties living across different parts of the UK — urban and rural, different regions — who all eat meat. I'll frame the session as a conversation about their everyday lives around food: what they eat, where they eat, who they eat with. I'll keep the collective framing practical and grounded rather than abstract — 'men talking about food and how they live' — so it stays accessible and doesn't prime self-consciousness about masculinity before that topic arises organically.
priority_research_areas: Gender and food choice (Section 3): This is the section most likely to produce socially desirable or performative answers — participants may either overstate gender's irrelevance ('I just eat what I want') or lean into stereotypes. Behavioural grounding will be essential: moving from stated attitudes to concrete recent moments.

Plant-based eating as a hypothetical (Section 4): The 'imagine going plant-based' framing risks abstract wishlist answers. The challenge will be pressing for specificity — what would actually need to change in their real lives, their social routines, their relationships — rather than general barriers.

Social acceptability and gendered meanings around food (cutting across Sections 3–5): Participants may reference what 'other men' think while not acknowledging their own role in those norms. Watching for third-person distancing and surfacing it without embarrassing anyone will be a live challenge throughout.

Consensus risk across the group: All five are meat-eating men of similar ages. There is a real risk of fast convergence — especially on plant-based eating as impractical or 'not for us' — that could shut down richer individual variation early. Active dissent-inviting will likely be needed in Sections 4 and 5.

participant_notes.anticipated_role: At 20, Amir is the youngest by four years. He may be somewhat quieter in a group where others are slightly older, or conversely may try to assert himself. Worth monitoring whether he self-selects out of questions that feel more 'settled adult life' oriented.
participant_notes.initial_attention_flag: Youngest participant — watch for signs of deference to older voices; create entry points for him specifically in later sections if he goes quiet.

participant_notes.anticipated_role: 27, urban Scotland. No specific profile flags. May represent a different food culture / dietary context to the English participants — worth watching for regional texture in his answers.

Ibrahim is 24, North East urban. As a Muslim name, there is a possibility of halal food practices shaping his relationship to meat and plant-based eating — this is not assumed but may emerge. If it does, it could add important texture to how religious or cultural identity intersects with food choice.
participant_notes.initial_attention_flag: Cultural/religious food context may emerge — follow naturally if raised, don't prompt it.

participant_notes.anticipated_role: Isaiah, 26, Yorkshire. No specific flags. Yorkshire urban setting — may have views shaped by a strong regional food culture. Monitor for whether he becomes a dominant voice given no obvious reticence signals.

Will, 29, rural Scotland — the only rural participant and the oldest. Rural context likely means a different relationship to food sourcing, land, and possibly hunting/game. This could be a distinctively different perspective that, if surfaced, should be given room. He may also feel slightly set apart from the urban majority.
participant_notes.initial_attention_flag: Only rural participant — his perspective on food may be structurally different; give him space to articulate that difference if he signals it.

known_risk_conditions: Social desirability bias is high on gender and masculinity topics — men may present themselves as unconcerned by gender norms even when behaviour suggests otherwise. Use behavioural grounding (specific recent events, social situations) rather than attitude questions alone.

Group may converge quickly on 'taste', 'convenience', and 'cost' as the only food decision factors — plan probes that push into social context and identity before the group settles on a simple shared answer.
Plant-based eating may be dismissed quickly with shared mockery or performative resistance — watch for this early in Section 4 and have a dissent-invitation or sharpening move ready.

Third-person distancing is a likely pattern ('other men would feel weird about it') — when participants attribute attitudes to 'other men' rather than themselves, probe gently for their own position without forcing them to abandon the distancing frame entirely.

With five men of similar ages all eating meat, group identity consolidation could happen early — the shared identity may create in-group pressure that suppresses honest individual variation. Stay alert to this from Section 2 onward.
initial_session_plan.directivity_plan: Sections 0–1 (intro and context): Light touch. Let the conversation warm up. Probe only if something unexpectedly rich emerges — don't exhaust rapport-building time on depth. Section 2 (everyday food decision-making): Moderate directivity. Push past the obvious (taste, convenience) into social context and specific situations, but don't force it. This section lays the groundwork for Section 3. Section 3 (gender and food choice): Increase directivity significantly. This is the first main topic section and the one most at risk of social performance. Use behavioural grounding, direct probes on specific moments, and dissent invitations if convergence appears. Section 4 (plant-based shift): High directivity. The hypothetical framing needs to be anchored in real life specifics — push for concrete changes, not abstract barriers. This section is where the most important research data will be generated. Section 5 (making plant-based foods more appealing): Moderate-to-high directivity. The risk here is generic advertising-style answers. Probe for specific personal resonance and social context rather than marketing wish-lists. Section 6 (closing): Light. Give room for anything that hasn't been said, then close warmly.

time_budget.budget_rationale: Main topic sections (3, 4, 5) carry the research weight and receive the largest allocations — together approximately 60% of total budget. Context sections (1, 2) receive moderate allocations as warm-up and grounding phases. Intro (0) and closing (6) are kept lean — enough to set up and close down, not enough to exhaust participants before the core discussion begins.

per_section.section_label: Opening discussion: male friendship and place

discussion_guide.scripted_question:
Hi everyone, thanks so much for joining the focus group today. We’re
going to take about 45 minutes to talk about your food choices and
opinions, and this will be recorded for research purposes. Try not to
overthink the questions, and simply speak freely. There are no right
or wrong answers. Please be respectful of your fellow focus group
members, and keep your responses relatively brief to allow time for
everyone to speak. But remember that this is a conversation, not an
interview, so you can jump in when you have something to say and you
don’t have to take turns answering each question, but you can if you
want to. Okay great, let’s start by going around and saying your name
and where in the UK you’re coming from today.

discussion_guide.section_label: Opening discussion: male friendship and place
discussion_guide.section_purpose: Section 1: Opening discussion: male friendship and place
discussion_guide.scripted_question:
What’s your favourite place in your city to spend time with your male
friends? Why? Feel free to be specific.
How do you decide what to eat?
suggested_probes: Do other people influence what you eat? If so, tell us more about how.
Do your work or hobbies influence what foods you eat? Tell us more about how.
How important is health and nutrition?

discussion_guide.scripted_question:
Do you think your gender influences what you eat? Tell us more about
why or why not.
suggested_probes: Is it socially acceptable for men to eat vegetarian or vegan foods?

discussion_guide.scripted_question:
Imagine you decided to go plant-based — what would need to change in
your life for you to do that?
suggested_probes: How would your family and friends react to this?
How might it change the way you shop or cook?

discussion_guide.section_purpose: Section 5: Making plant-based foods more appealing
discussion_guide.scripted_question:
What might make plant-based foods more appealing to you or other men
you know?

Okay everyone, that’s our time. Thanks so much for participating
today. Before we finish, is there anything else you would like to add
about food choices, gender, masculinity, or plant-based eating?

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section was purely introductory — participants shared names, ages, and locations. The group spans urban and rural UK contexts (North East, Birmingham, Leeds, Glasgow, rural Scotland), with ages clustered in the mid-to-late twenties. No substantive themes emerged yet beyond a light geographic contrast between Will's rural Scotland background and the urban majority. The section closed with the first substantive prompt about go-to social spaces.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The priority was a smooth, low-pressure opening — establishing a conversational rather than formal register and ensuring all five participants were heard before moving on. One proactive prompt was needed to bring in David, who hadn't volunteered. That worked cleanly. Holding the transition to the first real question until everyone had introduced themselves was the right call; the group settled quickly and the atmosphere felt relaxed.

section_summaries.section_label: Opening discussion: male friendship and place
section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section centred on the tension between anonymity and belonging in urban versus rural socialising. A recurring theme was the value of 'chosen visibility' — the city middle ground where you know people but aren't obligated to engage. Will's rural counter-perspective introduced the idea that anonymity carries a loneliness cost, while community surveillance carries a belonging benefit. The group largely converged on Ibrahim's framing of a productive middle ground, with David and Will's initial contrast doing most of the generative work.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The priority was widening a productive two-person exchange between David and Will before it exhausted itself, then systematically drawing in the three urban participants to test whether the emerging framework held across cities. Both interventions worked cleanly — Ibrahim and then Isaiah and Amir added texture without simply agreeing. The closing synthesis was probably slightly neat given Isaiah and Amir's contributions were thin; nudging for more before transitioning might have been worthwhile.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section centred on how geography shapes food decision-making — the contrast between urban convenience-as-invisibility (Ibrahim) and rural constraint-as-knowledge (Will), with David occupying a mid-point. A recurring tension emerged between unconscious habit and structural context: participants largely ate meat by default, but the reasons differed. Will reframed constraint positively through provenance and community relationship, complicating a simple urban/rural hierarchy rather than just reproducing it.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The priority was establishing baseline food behaviours before probing attitudes — letting the Ibrahim/Will exchange develop naturally before intervening to draw in the three silent participants. The intervention worked partially: David contributed a useful middle-ground position, but Isaiah and Amir still haven't spoken this section. The transition to the gender question was perhaps slightly premature given two participants remain unheard on the opening question; their absence risks compounding.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section centred on the distinction between social noticeability and identity meaning — whether vegetarianism would merely be 'different' or would carry a masculine charge. Isaiah and Amir worked toward separating habit from gender performance, with Amir ultimately revising his earlier balance-framing to acknowledge a 'safe choice' logic. Will complicated the urban consensus by arguing rural fixed identity removes the performance element entirely, reframing anonymity as the precondition for food choices becoming masculine statements.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The priority was activating Isaiah and Amir, who had been silent across the previous section, and the transition question achieved that cleanly — both engaged substantively and drove the most conceptually generative exchange of the session. Redirecting mid-section to bring in Will, Ibrahim, and David was the right call; Will's rural pushback meaningfully sharpened the emerging framework. Ibrahim and David remain unheard this section, which is a compounding gap worth monitoring entering the next.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section deepened the earlier safe-choice framework into a more reflexive register: the central tension shifted from whether meat-eating carries masculine charge to what happens once that logic becomes visible. Isaiah and Amir converged on a paradox — awareness increases the cost of changing rather than dissolving it, because the default becomes a conscious choice you must own. Ibrahim's counter-position complicated this: for him, the behaviour simply isn't loaded, offering a third mode beyond performance and critical awareness.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The priority was redirecting a productive Isaiah–Amir exchange to the three unheard participants before it became self-contained. The intervention worked partially — Ibrahim contributed a genuinely distinct position rather than just affirming. Will and David were not reached before the transition, which the closing prompt acknowledged by folding them into the next section's opening. Signalling the upcoming topic shift while asking for quick additions was a reasonable compression, though it risks Will and David contributing only superficially.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section centred on a chicken-and-egg problem: accessibility and social normalisation are mutually dependent, neither sufficient alone. Will's veg-box example became a productive flashpoint — Ibrahim and Isaiah argued it demonstrated social capital rather than accessibility as the operative mechanism, complicating Will's incrementalist optimism. The urban/rural contrast from earlier sections sharpened here into a question about whether city communities can generate the embedded trust that makes new behaviours unremarkable without anyone consciously choosing to normalise them.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The priority was drawing in David and Isaiah, who had been peripheral in recent sections — both were reached through direct address and contributed usefully, David offering a nuanced neither/nor position. The Will–Amir–Ibrahim exchange was allowed to develop before intervening, which paid off in a genuinely generative three-way tension. The closing open invitation was a reasonable way to signal session end without abruptly cutting off, though it risks producing thin additions rather than substantive new material.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section ended on a single, brief exchange that shifted the conversation's register from structural analysis to personal accountability. The dominant theme was the gap between externalising barriers and acknowledging agency — Amir's self-diagnosis that identifying social blockers had functioned as a way of avoiding personal commitment. This extended the earlier safe-choice and critical-awareness frameworks by adding a reflexive final layer: knowing the logic doesn't dissolve it, but it does remove the excuse.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: This was a closing section requiring little intervention — Amir arrived at a genuinely integrative position unprompted, and the moderator's role was simply to affirm it and close cleanly. The brief reflection in the moderator's closing turn worked as a light synthesis without overstating. The trade-off is that Will, David, Ibrahim, and Isaiah were not heard in this final section; the close prioritised quality of ending over participation balance, which was reasonable given time constraints.

The most important thing I'd say upfront is that this is genuinely a conversation — I'm not looking for right answers, and there isn't a hidden correct position I'm trying to get you all to land on. I'm interested in what you actually think and do, even when that's ordinary or a bit contradictory, because that's where the interesting stuff usually is. And if you disagree with each other, that's completely fine, actually really useful. Try not to overthink it — just speak from your own experience as much as you can. Okay, let's start simple — let's go around and if everyone could say your name and where in the UK you're coming from today, that'd be great.
I'm Ibrahim, by the way. I'm from the North East, urban area. Twenty-four. Cheers for having me.
Yeah, cheers. I'm Amir, twenty, from Birmingham — West Midlands. Urban as well, so yeah. Cheers for having me too.
Yeah, cheers. I'm Isaiah, twenty-six, from Yorkshire — urban area, Leeds. Cheers for having me as well.
Yeah, cheers. I'm Will, twenty-nine, from rural Scotland. So a bit different from you lot, I reckon. Nice to meet everyone.
Great, nice to have you all here. David, I don't think we've heard from you yet?
Yeah, cheers. I'm David, twenty-seven, from urban Scotland — Glasgow actually, so Will, we're basically neighbours, just different ends. Nice to meet you all.

You can sit, have a drink, chat about whatever. Football, work, what's going on. Don't really need to plan it that much.

I guess what works about it is it's just... normal. Nobody's trying to perform anything or prove anything. You're just there with mates. Could be talking about something serious one minute, then someone cracks a joke and you move on. That's kind of it for me.

Yeah, I get that — the pub thing. But it's a bit different where I am, to be honest. Like, there's a pub in the village, right, and that's where people go, but it's not quite the same as what you're describing. Everyone knows everyone, so you can't just sort of... blend in, you know? There's always someone's mum or your old teacher in there, or someone who'll tell your mum you were there. It's less about just being normal and more about being seen being normal, if that makes sense.

We do end up there, and it's fine, but a lot of the time we're just driving somewhere else — nearest proper town, or just out doing something. You've got to be a bit more intentional about it because there's not much else around. So it's less casual than what you're saying, I think.

Yeah, that makes sense. That's a different thing entirely, isn't it — when you can't actually just be anonymous. I hadn't really thought about it that way, but you're right. In the city you've got that luxury where you can walk into a pub and nobody's clocking who you are or reporting back to anyone. You're just... there.

I think that does change things. Like, when Will says being seen being normal — that's a pressure, isn't it? Even if it sounds like a small thing. Because then you're managing how you come across the whole time. Whereas in the pub round mine, you can just be a bit messy, a bit loud, whatever. Nobody cares because it's not a statement about anything. It's just what you're doing that night.

I'd probably go a bit mad if I had to be that conscious about it every time I went out with mates. Fair play for dealing with that, honestly.

Yeah, but I dunno — it cuts both ways, doesn't it? Like, yeah, there's the pressure thing you're saying. But in a village everyone also just... knows you. Like, people aren't judging you the same way because they've known you since you were a kid. Your mates' parents know your parents. There's less of that performance because people already know what you're actually like.

Whereas if I'm honest, the anonymity thing you're describing sounds a bit lonely to me. You can be messy and loud and nobody cares, but also nobody really knows you, you know? If you have a rough time or something's going on, the pub round here — everyone just sort of... notices. People check in. It's annoying sometimes, but it's also not nothing.

I'm not saying one's better than the other. But I think there's something about the city thing where you get freedom but maybe you lose something else. I'm not sure anonymity is actually as good as it sounds when you're describing it like that.

There's enough people around that you're not getting clocked all the time, but you're also not completely invisible.

I get what Ibrahim's saying though about the middle ground. That's probably more accurate for Glasgow actually. You get both — you know people, but there's also enough going on that you're not the focus of everyone's attention. And yeah, like he said, it's not just lads all doing the same thing. You see different people, different ages. That probably does make it feel less like you're performing for one specific idea of what you're supposed to be.

There's enough people around that you're not getting watched all the time, but you're also not completely invisible either. You know your locals, the people who work there, some regulars, but there's loads of other people coming through so nobody's really clocking your every move.

I think what David said about having a choice resonates with me though. Like, I can go to a pub near mine and know people, or I can just go somewhere else if I want a bit more... I dunno, space maybe? Without it being this whole thing. And I think that matters more than I'd probably admit — just knowing you don't have to perform or explain yourself if you don't want to.

But I get what Will's saying as well about the loneliness thing. I reckon that's fair.
